metadata.title: The Stateful Bottleneck
metadata.purpose: STEM & AI Architecture, Week 8 — stateless authentication: why server-side sessions bottleneck distributed systems, what a JWT actually contains, how independent services verify without a shared database, and the revocation cost that buys.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal, and this video is about why modern microservices do not remember who you are. Traditionally, when you logged into a website, the server kept a record of your session in its memory. But in an era of distributed agents and services scaling to millions of requests, remembering every active user becomes an expensive bottleneck.

beats.narration_text: A stateless token moves the proof of who you are out of the server's memory and into your own hands — signed, so it cannot be forged. You stop asking a database and start checking a signature.

beats.narration_text: The solution is stateless authentication, most commonly implemented with JSON Web Tokens. Instead of the server storing a record of your login, it cryptographically signs a digital passport and hands it to you. It says: I verify this user is an admin, and this passport expires in thirty minutes.

props.command: Split this JWT into its three parts and show me which of them a client could read without holding any key.

beats.authoring_note: ASK → RESULT pair: BASK is the ask, B03 is the result (ASK→RESULT LAW).

beats.narration_text: A JWT has three parts. The header names the algorithm. The payload carries the claims — your identity, your role, the expiry. And the signature is the cryptographic lock. But note what that means. The payload is encoded, not encrypted. Anyone holding the token can read it. What they cannot do is change it, because the signature would stop matching. The server checks the maths instead of checking a database.
beats.new_visual_element: The token, split, with the part everyone misreads

beats.honesty_note: ADDITION TO THE SCRIPT. The script describes the three parts but not that the payload is base64url-ENCODED, not encrypted — the most common and most dangerous misreading of JWTs, and the reason secrets must never be placed in a payload. The token string shown is illustrative, not a real signed token.

beats.narration_text: This changes the architecture. You can have fifty services on fifty machines, and each verifies the same token independently, without ever calling a central database. But note how they verify. Not with a shared secret — give fifty services the key that signs tokens and any one of them can mint an admin token for all the others. They hold a public key, which verifies signatures and cannot create them.
beats.new_visual_element: Three services, verifying in parallel, sharing nothing

beats.honesty_note: DELIBERATE CORRECTION. The script says the services work 'as long as they all share the same secret key'. Sharing one HMAC secret across N services means any one of them can MINT tokens for all the others — one compromise forges admin everywhere. The correct multi-service pattern is asymmetric signing (RS256/ES256): the issuer holds the private key, verifiers hold only the public key. The reel teaches that and says why. The script's 'infinitely scalable' is also scoped — removing the session lookup does not remove rate limits, network or compute.
beats.authoring_note: Uses the new connectors:false prop. Connectors would assert a sequence, and this beat's whole claim is that the three verify INDEPENDENTLY.

beats.narration_text: So where does this break? You cannot take a token back. A session you delete server-side and the user is out instantly. A signed token stays valid until it expires, because nothing looks anything up — that was the entire point. Steal one and it works until the clock runs out. Which is why short expiries and a refresh flow are not optional extras. They are the price of statelessness.

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED — the script has no falsifiability scene (HOOK / SOLUTION / DECODING / SYNERGY / TASK). The ai-explainer teaching arc requires one, and revocation is the genuine cost of statelessness: the same property that removes the lookup removes the kill switch. Reuses ThreeStageBand's failure mode.

beats.narration_text: So stop overloading your database with session checks. Use signed tokens to distribute trust across your architecture — and set the expiry deliberately, because that number is your entire blast radius.

props.title: verify.py
props.code:
jwt.decode(
    token,
    PUBLIC_KEY,          # not a shared secret
    algorithms=["RS256"],
)

# TASK: shift to stateless architecture.

# Then set exp deliberately.
# A stolen token is valid for exactly
# that long — exp IS your blast radius.

beats.authoring_note: Shows RS256 with a public key rather than a shared secret, consistent with the B04 correction. The expiry comment ties the task to the falsifiability beat.

beats.narration_text: And here is the prompt worth running on your own system. Ask a model what an attacker could do with one of your tokens for its full lifetime, assuming they cannot forge it and you cannot revoke it. The answer is your real exposure, and it is usually larger than the expiry number suggests.

props.command: Here are my JWT claims and my token expiry. Assume an attacker steals one valid token and I cannot revoke it. List everything they can do before it expires, ranked by damage — and tell me which claim I should not be putting in there at all.

beats.narration_text: Stop asking the database who someone is. Check the signature — and watch the clock. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
